sec.title: Purpose
sec.p: Heart failure (HF) management is well-defined for reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) but less so for mildly reduced (HFmrEF) or preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). This meta-analysis evaluates the impact of Finerenone, a nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, on cardiovascular and renal outcomes in these patient populations.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A systematic search in PubMed and Embase identified randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on Finerenone’s cardiovascular and renal effects. Three RCTs were included—FIDELIO-DKD, FIGARO-DKD, and FINEARTS-HF—encompassing 19,027 participants. Primary outcomes included cardiovascular death, HF hospitalization, and renal failure. Secondary outcomes focused on safety and adverse events like acute kidney injury and hyperkalemia. Meta-analyses were performed using hazard ratios (HR), confidence intervals (CI), and Relative Risk (RR).

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Finerenone was associated with a 20% reduction in HF hospitalization risk (HR 0.80, 95% CI: 0.72–0.90) and a 14% reduction in all-cause mortality (RR 0.86, 95% CI: 0.77–0.97). Finerenone did not significantly reduce cardiovascular death (HR 0.91, 95% CI: 0.82–1.01, p = 0.06). Renal failure rates were similar between Finerenone and placebo (RR 1.05, 95% CI: 0.65–1.68). Hyperkalemia incidence was significantly higher with Finerenone, with a RR of 2.31 (95% CI: 1.98–2.69).

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This meta-analysis shows that Finerenone significantly reduces HF hospitalizations and all-cause mortality in patients with chronic kidney disease and heart failure. Further studies are needed to clarify its effects on cardiovascular death and renal failure.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) and Heart Failure (HF) are two of the most common chronic diseases in the United States with a prevalence of 35.5 million and 6.7 million, respectively [1, 2]. These two conditions are inherently connected and affect each other bidirectionally. Patients with CKD are more likely to die from cardiovascular disease than to progress to end-stage renal disease [3]. Accordingly, the emerging concept of the Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic syndrome [4] is gaining increasing traction, further illustrating the physiologic link between the cardiac and renal systems. The associated healthcare costs with these conditions are significant, with 23.5% of Medicare spending being devoted to patients with CKD in 2020, signifying a need for improved long-term management [5].

The pharmacologic management of Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF) is well-documented. In the 2022 American College of Cardiology guidelines for management of heart failure, four pillars of pharmacotherapy have Class 1(A) evidence: Renin-Angiotensin System (RAS) inhibitors, beta-blockers, steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors. In contrast, the management of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF) is less defined. For these populations, the guidelines provide a Class 1 (B-NR) recommendation for diuretics as needed across all types of heart failure, and a Class 2a (B-R) recommendation for SGLT2 inhibitors specifically for HFpEF and HFmrEF [6]. As such, more research is needed to further investigate optimal therapy for these conditions.

On the other hand, the newest iteration of the Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) guidelines for chronic kidney disease was published in 2024 [7]. Of interest, these guidelines now support add-on therapy with the non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, Finerenone, for patients with CKD in the setting of sub optimally controlled Diabetes Mellitus (DM) type 2 on maximally-tolerated RAS blockade. This new recommendation is based upon two main trials: Effects of Finerenone on Chronic Kidney Disease Outcomes in Type 2 Diabetes (FIDELIO-DKD) and Cardiovascular Events with Finerenone in Kidney Disease and Type 2 Diabetes (FIGARO-DKD) [8, 9]. Subsequent to the publication of these trials showcasing the effect of Finerenone on CKD, a third trial named Finerenone in Heart Failure with Mildly Reduced or Preserved Ejection Fraction (FINEARTS-HF) was conducted to evaluate the effects of Finerenone on HFmrEF and HFpEF. Therefore, we conducted this meta-analysis to further evaluate the effects of the novel nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist as a new treatment option for HFmrEF and HFpEF.

sec.title: Data Source and Searches
sec.p:
We followed the PRISMA guidelines [10] and have summarized our search process in Fig. 1. Adhering to the PRISMA checklist, we ensured comprehensive and transparent reporting of our systematic review, as seen in the supplementary file. Two investigators (JC.RM, and M.S.) developed the search strategy, which was revised and approved by the other investigators. We searched the following databases until September 1, 2024: PubMed-MEDLINE and EMBASE-OVID. The search strategy is shown in the supplementary file. There was no language limitation. Fig. 1
PRISMA flow diagram

sec.title: Study Selection
sec.p: We included only RCTs in English reporting cardiovascular outcomes of Finerenone as treatment versus placebo. We excluded studies that did not match our population, intervention, and outcomes. Three investigators (JC.RM, M.S., and A.K.) independently screened each record title and abstract for potential inclusion. They then assessed the full texts of selected abstracts. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion or by another investigator (A.B.).

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: The primary outcomes included death from cardiovascular causes, hospitalization for heart failure, death from any cause, and renal failure. The secondary outcomes focused on safety and adverse events, which included any serious adverse event, acute kidney injury, investigator-reported hyperkalemia, hyperkalemia related to the trial regimen, urinary tract infections, and pneumonia.

sec.title: Data Extraction
sec.p: Three investigators (JC.RM., M.S., A.K.) independently extracted data on the following variables: study design, study population, intervention group size, control group size, primary outcomes, secondary outcomes, and follow-up duration. Discrepancies in data extraction were resolved by discussion or by another investigator (A.B.). Baseline characteristics included demographics, clinical history, laboratory values, and medication use. Specifically, we summarized age, sex distribution, and racial composition (White, Black, Asian, Other, with missing data noted). Clinical history included duration of diabetes, systolic blood pressure, and the presence of cardiovascular disease. Kidney function was assessed using estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), categorized into ≥ 60, 45 to < 60, 25 to < 45, and < 25 ml/min/1.73 m2. The urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio was reported as a median with interquartile range (IQR) and categorized into < 30, 30 to < 300, and ≥ 300, including missing data. Baseline serum potassium levels were measured in mmol/liter. Medication use at baseline was recorded, including the use of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers, other renin-angiotensin system inhibitors, diuretics, statins, potassium-lowering agents, glucose-lowering therapies (including insulin, glucagon-like-peptide-1 receptor agonists and sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors). Further details on these characteristics are provided in the baseline characteristics section.

sec.title: Risk of Bias Assessment
sec.p: Two investigators (M.S. and A.K.), independently assessed the risk of bias (RoB) by using the Cochrane RoB 2.0 tool for RCTs [11]; disagreements were resolved by discussion with a third investigator (A.B.). RoB 2.0 evaluates five bias domains: randomization process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of the outcome, and selection of the reported result. The risk of bias assessment can be viewed in the supplementary file.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Our systematic review followed the 2020 PRISMA guidelines [10], and the analyses were conducted using the meta package in RevMan [12]. For the primary outcomes, we used a generic inverse variance random effects model, analyzing logged hazard ratios (HR) and confidence intervals (CI) for the two outcomes: death from cardiovascular causes and hospitalization for heart failure, as all three studies provided HRs for these measures. For death from any cause and renal failure, we employed a dichotomous random effects model, reporting outcomes as risk ratios (RR) because the FINEARTS-HF study did not provide HRs for these outcomes [13]. Adverse events were also analyzed as dichotomous outcomes using a random effects model and reported as RR.

We assessed heterogeneity among studies using the I2 statistic, with I2 values greater than 60% indicating substantial heterogeneity. The quality of evidence was determined using the GRADE methodology, which examines five key domains: risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias [14]. Publication bias was not assessed with Egger’s test, given a likely unreliable result with only three studies [15].

sec.title: Selection of Studies
sec.p: Three studies were included in the final analysis and Fig. 1 shows the study selection process.

sec.title: Characteristics of Included Studies
sec.p:
The study characteristics are summarized in Table 1. The FIDELIO-DKD and FIGARO-DKD studies involved patients with CKD and type 2 diabetes mellitus, administering finerenone at 10 mg daily for eGFR 25–60 mL/min/1.73 m2 and 20 mg for those above 60 mL/min/1.73 m2. FIDELIO-DKD enrolled 5,674 participants, while FIGARO-DKD included 7,352. The FINEARTS-HF study, which focused on HFmrEF and HFpEF, enrolled 6,001 participants, administering finerenone at 20 mg daily for eGFR 30–60 mL/min/1.73 m2 and 40 mg for higher eGFR. In total, 19,027 participants were included across the studies. Primary outcomes generally included kidney failure, cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, stroke, and heart failure hospitalization, with secondary outcomes examining kidney function and heart failure symptom changes over follow-up periods of 31.2 to 40.8 months (Table 1). sec.title: Baseline Characteristics
sec.p:
The baseline characteristics are summarized in Table 2. The Effects of Finerenone on Chronic Kidney Disease Outcomes in Type 2 Diabetes (FIDELIO-DKD) and Cardiovascular Events with Finerenone in Kidney Disease and Type 2 Diabetes (FIGARO-DKD) studies focused on patients with chronic kidney disease and type 2 diabetes mellitus, with participants typically having moderate to severe kidney impairment (eGFR 25–60 mL/min/1.73 m2) and a majority presenting with albuminuria. Many were already on renin-angiotensin system inhibitors [8, 9]. The populations in these studies were mostly older adults, averaging in their mid-60 s, with a majority being male. In the Finerenone in Heart Failure with Mildly Reduced or Preserved Ejection Fraction (FINEARTS-HF) trial, targeting HFmrEF and HFpEF patients, participants had eGFRs ranging from 30–60 mL/min/1.73 m2 in the lower dose group and above 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 in the higher dose group [13]. This group had high rates of comorbidities, including hypertension and dyslipidemia. Overall, the trial populations were well-balanced between treatment and control arms, with no significant differences in key characteristics, allowing for a fair comparison of outcomes. Table 2

sec.title: Risk of Bias of Included Studies
sec.p: Risk of bias analysis indicated a low risk of bias across all domains for the FIDELIO-DKD, FIGARO-DKD, and FINEARTS-HF studies. Specifically, there was a low risk of bias related to the randomization process, deviations from the intended intervention, missing outcome data, measurement of the outcome, and selection of the reported result. The overall risk of bias was judged to be low for all studies. The GRADE approach determined high certainty for most outcomes except for kidney failure, which was rated as moderate certainty due to high heterogeneity (I2 > 60%). These details are in the supplementary file.

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p:
Finerenone reduced the risk of heart failure hospitalization by 20% (RR: 0.80, 95% CI: 0.72–0.90, p < 0.0001, I2 = 0%). Additionally, it was associated with a significant reduction in all-cause mortality (RR: 0.86, 95% CI: 0.77–0.97, p = 0.01, I2 = 0%). There were no significant differences observed in the risk of renal failure (RR: 1.05, 95% CI: 0.65–1.68, p = 0.80, I2 = 83%) or death from cardiovascular causes (HR: 0.91, 95% CI: 0.82–1.01, p = 0.08, I2 = 0%). However, substantial heterogeneity was noted among the studies in these outcomes. The primary outcomes are summarized in Table 3 and represented in the forest plots in Fig. 2. For any serious adverse event, Finerenone was associated with a 5% risk reduction compared to the control group (RR: 0.95, 95% CI 0.91–0.98, p = 0.005, I2 = 0%). However, there was a statistically significant increase in hyperkalemia related to the trial regimen (RR: 2.31, 95% CI: 1.98–2.69, p < 0.0001, I2 = 0%) and investigator-reported hyperkalemia (RR: 2.09, 95% CI: 1.90–2.30, p < 0.0001, I2 = 0%). Finerenone did not show a significant effect on the incidence of acute kidney injury (RR: 1.10, 95% CI: 0.78–1.53, p = 0.60, I2 = 67%), with considerable heterogeneity noted. Similarly, there was no significant difference in the risk of urinary tract infection between groups (RR: 1.00, 95% CI: 0.88–1.14, p = 0.98, I2 = 0%). Finally, Finerenone reduced the risk of heart failure by 28% (RR: 0.72, 95% CI: 0.63–0.82, p < 0.0001, I2 = 0%).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This meta-analysis combined data from three major RCTs evaluating the efficacy of Finerenone in patients with CKD and associated heart failure, especially with HFmrEF and HFpEF. The key finding of our study is that Finerenone significantly decreases the risk of hospitalization for heart failure by 20 percent. This result was of special interest because evidence-based therapeutic options for HFmrEF and HFpEF are limited. Further evidence of the potential role of Finerenone as a useful therapeutic agent in this population is represented by the 14 percent reduction in all-cause mortality. On the other hand, the effectiveness of Finerenone on cardiovascular mortality did not attain statistical significance. Therefore, this finding shows that although Finerenone may reduce heart failure hospitalizations along with all-cause mortality, it does not change cardiovascular-specific mortality overall. Additionally, there was no statistically significant effect on renal failure outcomes across the studies. These may relate to the various populations studied, particularly those trials that included patients with different stages of CKD and different severities of heart failure. However, all the included studies have a reasonable sample size, high design quality, and low risk of bias.

The non-significant findings for cardiovascular mortality in this meta-analysis warrant further consideration. One possible explanation could be the duration of follow-up in the included studies. Cardiovascular mortality outcomes may require a longer observation period to capture the full benefits of Finerenone, especially given its gradual effects on reducing fibrosis and inflammation in cardiovascular tissues [16]. Shorter follow-up durations may limit the ability to detect statistically significant changes in cardiovascular mortality, as these outcomes typically evolve over a longer timeframe compared to hospitalization rates.

Additionally, variations in patient characteristics across the studies, including baseline cardiovascular risk and the severity of CKD, could influence these findings. Patients with more advanced cardiovascular disease or differing comorbidities may experience varied responses to Finerenone, potentially impacting overall cardiovascular mortality outcomes. Furthermore, the background therapies that patients were receiving, such as standard heart failure treatments and other renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system inhibitors, may have also contributed to the non-significant results by partially overlapping with Finerenone’s effects. These factors underscore the need for future research with extended follow-up periods and potentially more homogeneous patient populations to better understand Finerenone’s long-term impact on cardiovascular mortality.

Recent literature supports these findings, as multiple meta-analyses in the past five years have evaluated the outcomes of Finerenone and other mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists in similar populations. For example, a meta-analysis compared Finerenone to SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists, showing that while SGLT2 inhibitors reduced the risk of kidney failure progression and heart failure hospitalization more effectively, all three therapies had comparable impacts on all-cause and cardiovascular mortality [17]. These studies align with our findings and emphasize the need for further research on the role of Finerenone in distinct heart failure subpopulations, such as those with HFmrEF and HFpEF.

While Finerenone demonstrates considerable promise in managing heart failure outcomes, its impact on atrial fibrillation, a major contributor to cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, remains unexplored. Current literature provides insight into the effects of mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists on atrial fibrillation. Notably, this analysis showed that while mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists like spironolactone significantly reduced atrial fibrillation events, Finerenone had a neutral effect​ [18]. This gap emphasizes the need for further research to evaluate whether Finerenone might offer protective benefits against atrial fibrillation in populations at high risk for related complications. Future studies examining Finerenone’s effect on atrial fibrillation could provide critical insights, especially as atrial fibrillation remains a major risk factor for stroke, heart failure, and overall cardiovascular morbidity.

The safety profile for Finerenone, as reflected in this meta-analysis, is mixed. While it reduces serious adverse events by 5 percent, it significantly increases the incidence of hyperkalemia. This side effect is consistent with the well-described pharmacologic effect of mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists. Hyperkalemia is a concerning adverse event, particularly in patients with CKD, and may limit the widespread use of Finerenone in this population. To mitigate this risk, careful patient selection is essential. For example, Finerenone may be better suited for patients with stable renal function and lower baseline potassium levels [19]. Additionally, implementing monitoring protocols, such as frequent serum potassium checks and adjusting Finerenone dosage based on renal function, could further reduce the risk of hyperkalemia [20]. Educating patients on dietary potassium restrictions and promptly managing any rises in potassium can also help maintain safety while maximizing Finerenone’s benefits [20]. These management strategies provide practical insights for clinicians aiming to incorporate Finerenone into their therapeutic arsenal safely.

These findings have clinical relevance given the increasing need for effective treatments in growing heart failure populations with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fractions. So far, treatment options for HFmrEF and HFpEF are lacking compared to well-established guidelines for HFrEF. Results of this meta-analysis suggest that Finerenone may fill this therapeutic gap by improving heart failure-related hospital admissions, but its limited impact on cardiovascular mortality and the significant risk of hyperkalemia must be carefully weighed. In light of these findings, it remains crucial to further review recent meta-analyses in this area to highlight how this adds to the existing literature.

Previous meta-analyses, such as those by Chen et al. [21], evaluated Finerenone against placebo or spironolactone but did not include the FINEARTS-HF trial. In contrast, the 2024 meta-analysis by Jhund et al. [22] included the latest trials; however, it was not specific to Finerenone, as it encompassed all mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) and only one study, FINEARTS-HF, focused on Finerenone. Therefore, our meta-analysis provides valuable insights into Finerenone’s specific role in heart failure treatment, particularly for patients with HFmrEF and HFpEF, addressing critical gaps left by prior studies.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: A significant limitation of our meta-analysis is the inclusion of FIDELIO-DKD and FIGARO-DKD, which focused primarily on patients with chronic kidney disease and diabetes mellitus, rather than explicitly diagnosed heart failure with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFpEF/HFmrEF). Although these trials excluded patients with symptomatic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF, NYHA class II-IV), they did not explicitly confirm that all included patients had heart failure, thus raising uncertainty about the presence and type of heart failure in these populations. However, FINEARTS-HF specifically included only patients with HFpEF or HFmrEF, ensuring that no HFrEF patients were included across any of the three studies.

We acknowledge that while the absence of HFrEF in all three studies is clear, it remains uncertain whether all patients in FIDELIO-DKD and FIGARO-DKD had a formal diagnosis of heart failure. Nevertheless, we included these trials in our analysis based on their shared outcome of "hospitalization for heart failure," which suggests a degree of overlap in patient populations with heart failure. Additionally, we included detailed breakdowns of baseline characteristics, where we stratified patient populations based on the available data regarding heart failure diagnoses.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Finerenone demonstrated a significant reduction in heart failure hospitalizations and all-cause mortality among patients with CKD and heart failure. However, its neutral impact on cardiovascular mortality, coupled with the risk of hyperkalemia, may limit its overall benefit. Future studies should aim to optimize the clinical use of Finerenone by specifying patient subgroups, particularly those with HFmrEF or HFpEF, who might derive the most benefit from this therapy. Research focusing exclusively on these populations could provide clarity on Finerenone’s role in addressing the limited treatment options for HFmrEF and HFpEF patients. Additionally, investigating combination strategies with other heart failure therapies could help mitigate the risk of hyperkalemia, enhancing the safety and efficacy profile of Finerenone in broader heart failure populations. Future trials with longer follow-up periods would also be valuable to fully understand Finerenone’s impact on cardiovascular mortality and long-term outcomes.
